correctness.rationale: An edge of the cubic host can dominate at most five edges, itself included; a maximal matching dominates all 36, so it needs at least eight. Independent increasing-edge recursion enumerated 293436 eight-edge matchings and tested maximality by exhaustion of all nonconflicting edges, including lower-numbered ones. Exactly 90 survive. Separate independent-set recursion gives 2964 possible omitted eight-sets, and the matching census has 90 distinct omissions with one completion each. All canonical states, all transitions, component lists, eccentricities and the two symmetry actions match the supplied certificate. Rotation acts as [1,2,0] and reflection as [0,2,1] on the three 30-state components, each four-regular and self-centered at five. The respective transition counts are 0,180,180,522. At four the graph is connected with degree profile 11:72,14:18 and eccentricity profile 3:18,4:72, proving the threshold and the stated radius and diameter.
residual_risks: The state graph requires optimal maximal matchings at step endpoints and permits simultaneous substitutions; no conclusion for sequential one-edge moves through nonoptimal states or other graph families.

value.rationale: On a standard cubic symmetric graph, the least simultaneous update budget for traversing every optimal matching answers a natural no-slack reconfiguration question. The exact obstruction is stronger than one-move freezing: two exchanges give three symmetric components, a third does not add a single edge, and four restore connectivity and bound travel. The complete state and transition data form an independently useful finite benchmark for minimum edge domination with the matching restriction.
residual_risks: No inference to general matching algorithms or to connectivity through nonoptimal states.
